title: Understanding the Challenges in Iterative Generative Optimization with LLMs
claim: Iterative optimization is a closed loop in which a system's feedback-bearing outputs drive an LLM optimizer to update the system.
layout: Single panel, bottom-up flow, red feedback loop arrow, green context box
description: A single small block diagram of the generative optimization learning loop. A light-green rounded region labeled "Learning Context" holds three parts. A blank white Input box feeds with a black arrow into an orange "Initial System" box. A black arrow goes up from the system to a blank white Output box, then another black arrow goes up to a purple "Feedback" box at the top. Outside the green region, a blue "LLM Optimizer" box sits at the bottom. A red arrow labeled "Update" goes from the optimizer up into the Initial System. A red arrow labeled "Loop" leaves the green region and returns to the optimizer. The eye goes first to the colored boxes, then follows the red arrows around the loop.
caption: The learning loop of generative optimization.
abstract: Generative optimization uses large language models (LLMs) to iteratively improve artifacts (such as code, workflows or prompts) using execution feedback. It is a promising approach to building self-improving agents, yet in practice remains brittle: despite active research, only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated optimization. We argue that this brittleness arises because, to set up a learning loop, an engineer must make "hidden" design choices: What can the optimizer edit and what is the ``right'' learning evidence to provide at each update? We investigate three factors that affect most applications: the starting artifact, the credit horizon for execution traces, and batching trials and errors into learning evidence. Through case studies in MLAgentBench, Atari, and BigBench Extra Hard, we find that these design decisions can determine whether generative optimization succeeds, yet they are rarely made explicit in prior work. Different starting artifacts determine which solutions are reachable in MLAgentBench, truncated traces can still improve Atari agents, and larger minibatches do not monotonically improve generalization on BBEH. We then study these factors jointly in harness optimization on TBLite, evaluated on Terminal-Bench 2.0. We also propose a batch-size and credit-horizon rule that, calibrated on TBLite, transfers to DeepSWE after adjusting to its token costs and comes within 1% of the best configuration tested at each context budget.
